prompt: Lesson 9. Fifty buyers each buy one seat at once. The code reads `sold`, adds one in Go and writes the result back, inside a transaction at PostgreSQL's default isolation. What is the outcome?

choices.text: Fewer seats recorded than sold
choices.why: Right. Two transactions read the same value and both write value plus one: a lost update.

choices.text: Exactly fifty, because each sale runs in its own transaction
choices.why: All or nothing is not isolation; at READ COMMITTED they still read each other's starting point.

choices.text: Forty-nine sales fail with SQLSTATE 40001
choices.why: Serialization failures come from REPEATABLE READ, not from the default level.

choices.text: The transactions deadlock and all fifty time out
choices.why: Plain reads take no locks; nothing waits, and that is the trouble.

prompt: Lesson 9. A colleague fixes the lost update by raising the isolation to REPEATABLE READ. Every count now adds up. What does the course hold against it?

choices.text: Buyers are refused with 40001 while seats are left
choices.why: Right. Each refusal is honest but needless; a single `UPDATE ... sold + 1` or `FOR UPDATE` sells to all of them.

choices.text: It makes every SELECT in the program take a write lock
choices.why: REPEATABLE READ takes no extra locks; it refuses the later writer instead.

choices.text: PostgreSQL does not offer that level
choices.why: It does; the lesson ran it.

choices.why: Right. The URL named no user, so pgx looked the uid up and found nothing; `postgres://$USER@/...` fixes it.

choices.text: Peer authentication refused the uid
choices.why: The server complained that no user name was sent, before any authentication.

choices.text: `DATABASE_URL` was not passed to the container

prompt: Lesson 16. A release script builds with `-ldflags "-X main.verison=v1.2.0"`. What does the binary report as its version?

choices.text: `dev`, and the build raised no error

choices.text: Nothing: the link fails

choices.text: An empty string

prompt: Lesson 17. A team's liveness check pings the database. The database goes down for five minutes. What follows?
hint: What does a "no" to liveness make the platform do?

choices.text: Traffic stops until the database returns, as it should
choices.why: That is what a readiness failure does; liveness kills.

choices.text: Every copy restarts in a loop
choices.why: Right. Restarts add load and fix nothing, since a restart does not bring the database back; that check belongs in readiness.

choices.text: Nothing, since liveness only runs at start-up
choices.why: That is a startup probe; liveness runs all the time.

choices.text: The database is restarted by the platform
choices.why: The platform acts on the process that answered, not on its dependencies.

prompt: Lesson 17. After PostgreSQL restarted, `/readyz` answered ready and every request worked, yet live pages stopped changing. Why did readiness miss it?
hint: Read the first log line of section 03.

choices.text: The pool lost all its connections for good
choices.why: The pool reopened them; requests worked.

choices.text: The trigger was dropped by the restart
choices.why: Restarting a server keeps its schema.

choices.text: `listen` was dead, unchecked
choices.why: Right. Nothing restarted `listen`, and readiness only pings; a health check checks what it is told; a reconnect loop and its state in readiness close the gap.

choices.text: The hub closed when readiness failed
choices.why: The hub closes only on shutdown.

prompt: Lesson 17. Without `RegisterOnShutdown(live.close)`, a viewer has the event page open when SIGTERM arrives. What happens to the shutdown?

choices.text: It ends at once; streams are idle connections
choices.why: A stream is mid-response, which is active.

choices.text: The process never exits
choices.why: The shutdown timeout bounds the wait.

choices.text: `EventSource` closes the stream when it sees 503
choices.why: The 503 is on the ops port; the page never asks it.

choices.text: It waits out the deadline
choices.why: Right. Eight seconds, then the stream is cut: a stream is a request built never to end.

prompt: Lesson 17. A service sets its shutdown timeout to 15 seconds and runs under `docker stop` with its default. A request in flight needs 12 seconds. What does it get?

choices.why: Right. The timeout must be shorter than the platform's grace, which is why boxoffice uses eight.

choices.text: A 503 from readiness
